cues.text: A Rival Council at Pisa
Pope Julius II had promised, on his election in 1503, to convoke a general council, but years passed without action.
In 1511, a group of dissident cardinals, backed by King Louis XII of France and Emperor Maximilian I , moved to force the pope's hand.
They convened their own council at Pisa , styling it a legitimate general council and summoning Julius himself to answer for his conduct.

Julius responded by declaring the Pisan assembly illegitimate and, on July 18, 1511, issuing the bull Sacrosanctae Romanae Ecclesiae summoning a properly convoked council of his own to the Lateran Basilica in Rome.
Military setbacks delayed the opening until the French victory at the Battle of Ravenna had passed; the council finally opened on May 3, 1512.
Condemning the Pisan Assembly

The council's early sessions, held under Julius II, focused on discrediting the rival Pisan gathering and revoking the French Pragmatic Sanction of Bourges , a 1438 decree that had long limited papal authority over the French Church.
Fifteen cardinals, the Latin Patriarchs of Alexandria and Antioch, ten archbishops, and fifty-six bishops attended the opening session.
By the standards of the great medieval councils, this was a modest showing but sufficient to establish the assembly's conciliar legitimacy against its Pisan rival.
Julius II died in February 1513, midway through the council's business, and his successor, Leo X , chose to continue rather than dissolve the assembly, presiding over its remaining seven sessions.
Reform and Doctrine Under Leo X

Under Leo X, the council turned to a broader program: negotiating a general peace among Christian rulers, addressing clerical discipline and reform, and confronting the intellectual currents of the Italian Renaissance.
Its most notable doctrinal act condemned philosophers who taught that the human soul was mortal or that all rational souls formed a single shared intellect.
These positions were associated with certain readings of Aristotle circulating in university faculties.
The act affirmed the individual immortality of each human soul as Catholic teaching.

The council also renewed regulation of preaching and reaffirmed decrees from Constance and Basel establishing papal primacy over conciliar authority, explicitly repudiating the stronger conciliarist claims that had briefly threatened papal supremacy in the previous century.
A Council Overtaken by Events

The council closed its twelfth and final session on March 16, 1517 , having planned a new crusade against the Ottoman Turks that never materialized for lack of the political unity such an expedition required.

Only months later, on October 31, 1517 , Martin Luther posted his Ninety-Five Theses at Wittenberg, setting in motion the Protestant Reformation the council had done little to anticipate or forestall.
In hindsight, many historians have judged Fifth Lateran's reform program too modest to address deeper structural grievances.
These concerns — around indulgences, clerical wealth, and doctrine — would soon fracture Western Christendom, while the program remained narrowly focused on internal Italian and curial matters.
Legacy

As the last ecumenical council before the Reformation, Fifth Lateran occupies an unenviable historical position: a genuine but ultimately insufficient attempt at reform, convened at precisely the moment when far more sweeping change was both needed and imminent.
It would be nearly three decades before the Church convened the next general council, now confronting a divided Christendom.
That council — the Council of Trent — carried a mandate for reform and doctrinal clarity far more urgent and far-reaching than anything Fifth Lateran had attempted.
